Gratitude may also be more general than praise, since praise is by the tongue, while gratitude is by the tongue, the heart, and the limbs. When you understand the generality of praise, you know that your saying "All praise is due to Allah" entails commending Him for His majesty, greatness, oneness, might, bounty, knowledge, capability, wisdom, and the other attributes, and it includes the meanings of His ninety-nine Most Beautiful Names. It also entails thanking Him and praising Him for every blessing He has given and every mercy He has granted to all His creatures in this world and the next. How wondrous is a word that gathers what volumes could not contain, and that the minds of all creatures cannot count! It is sufficient for you that Allah made it the beginning of His Book and the final call of the people of Paradise.

**The fourth benefit:** Gratitude by the tongue is praising the Benefactor and speaking of His blessings. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Speaking of blessings is gratitude." Gratitude by the limbs is acting in obedience to Allah and abstaining from His disobedience. Gratitude by the heart is knowing the magnitude of the blessing, knowing that it comes from Allah alone, and knowing that it is a bounty and not something the servant deserves. Know that the blessings for which gratitude is owed cannot be counted, but they fall into three categories: worldly blessings, such as health and wealth; religious blessings, such as knowledge and piety; and blessings of the Hereafter, which are His reward, abundant in recompense for a small deed in a short life. People differ in their gratitude on two levels. Some thank Allah only for the blessings that reach them specifically, while others thank Him on behalf of all His creatures for the blessings that reach all of them. Gratitude has three ranks: the rank of the common people is thanking Allah for blessings; the rank of the elite is thanking Him for blessings and afflictions and in every state; and the rank of the elite of the elite is to be absorbed away from the blessing by witnessing the Benefactor. A man said to Ibrāhīm ibn Adham: "When the poor are denied, they give thanks, and when they are given, they prefer others." Among the virtues of gratitude is that it is one of the attributes of the Real (al-Ḥaqq) and one of the attributes of creatures, for among Allah's names are al-Shākir (the Grateful) and al-Shakūr (the Most Grateful). I have explained both in the lexical section.

**The fifth benefit:** Our saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is, according to the verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqūn), superior to "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh), for two reasons. The first is what al-Nasā'ī recorded from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever says 'There is no god but Allah,' twenty good deeds are recorded for him, and whoever says 'All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds,' thirty good deeds are recorded for him." The second is that the monotheism entailed by "There is no god but Allah" is present in your saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, and your saying "All praise is due to Allah" adds to it, and it contains the meanings we have already mentioned. As for the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) saying: "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is 'There is no god but Allah,'" that refers to the monotheism it entails. The phrase "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" shares that with it and surpasses it. This believer says it seeking reward, but for one who has newly entered Islam, "There is no god but Allah" is required of him.

**The sixth benefit:** The word rabb (lord) is of the form fa'l with the vowel of the ʿayn being kasrah, and it has been contracted (udghima). Its meanings are four: the god (al-ilāh), the master (al-sayyid), the owner (al-mālik), and the one who sets things right (al-muṣliḥ). All of these apply to ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, but the stronger meaning is "god," because it is specific to Allah the Exalted. Likewise, the stronger view regarding al-ʿālamīn (the worlds) is that it refers to every existing thing other than Allah, encompassing all created beings.

**The seventh benefit:** The reading of the majority is مَلِكِ (Māliki, "King") without an alif, while ʿĀṣim and al-Kisā'ī read مَالِكِ (Mālik, "Owner") with an alif. The interpretation according to this reading is: "Owner of the coming of the Day of Judgment," or "Owner of the affair on the Day of Judgment." The reading of the majority is stronger for three reasons. First, the king (al-malik) is greater than the owner (al-mālik), since anyone may be described as an owner of his property, whereas the king is the lord of people. Second, Allah's saying: ﴿And His is the dominion on the Day the Horn is blown﴾. Third, the reading with mālik does not entail an omission, whereas the other reading does, because its implied meaning is "Owner of the affair" or "Owner of the coming of the Day of Judgment," and omission is contrary to the original form. As for the reading of the majority, the attribution of malik to yawm al-dīn is by way of broadening (al-ittisā'), and the time expression is treated as if it were a direct object, while the meaning is locative: the kingship over the Day of Judgment. It may also mean the kingship over affairs on the Day of Judgment, in which case there is an omission. Both readings have been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) in hadith. Malik has also been recited in many other ways, but these are irregular (shādhdhah).

**The eighth benefit:** al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, and Mālik are attributes (ṣifāt). If it is asked: how can Mālik be in the genitive as a qualifier of a definite noun, when the construct of an active participle is not pure (ghayr maḥḍah)? The answer: it is non-pure when it has the meaning of the present or the future, but this (ownership) is continuous and permanent, so its construct is pure (maḥḍah).

**The ninth benefit:** yawm al-dīn is the Day of Resurrection. It is apt here in the meanings of reckoning, recompense, and subjugation, as in Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, are we to be held accountable?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 53].

**The tenth benefit:** iyyāka in both places is an object of the verb that follows it. It was placed first to convey exclusivity (ḥaṣr), for fronting the objects entails exclusivity. So the servant's saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ requires that Allah alone be worshipped, without partner. His saying ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾ entails an acknowledgment of weakness and need, and that we seek help from Allah alone.

**The eleventh benefit:** ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ means: we ask You for assistance in worship and in all our affairs. This is evidence against the doctrines of the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah, and that the truth lies between them.

**The twelfth benefit:** ﴿Guide us﴾ is a supplication for guidance. If it is asked: how do believers ask for guidance when they already have it? The answer: this is a request for steadfastness upon it until death, or for an increase in it, for there is no limit to ascending through the stations.

**The thirteenth benefit:** Praise and commendation are placed before supplication, because that is the custom in supplication, and it is the nature of a request to come after praise, which is closer to being answered. Likewise, al-Raḥmān is placed before Mālik yawm al-dīn, because Allah's mercy precedes His wrath. Likewise, ﴿You alone we worship﴾ is placed before ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾, because the means is placed before the request for need.

**The fourteenth benefit:** Allah the Exalted is mentioned at the beginning of this sūrah in the third person (ghaybah), and then in the second person (khiṭāb) in ﴿You alone we worship﴾ and what follows. This is called iltifāt (shift of person), and it indicates that when the servant mentions Allah, he draws near to Him, and so becomes one of those in His presence, and He addresses him.

**The fifteenth benefit:** ṣirāṭ (path) in the lexical sense is the tangible road on which one walks. It was then borrowed for the path on which a person travels, whether good or evil. The meaning of mustaqīm (straight) is upright, with no crookedness in it. So ṣirāṭ mustaqīm is Islam, and it has been said it is the Qur'an. The two meanings are close, since the Qur'an contains the laws of Islam. Both have been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). The word ṣirāṭ has been recited with ṣād, with sīn, and with a sound between ṣād and zāy. It has also been said it was recited with a pure zāy. The original is sīn, but they changed it to ṣād to match the ṭā' in emphasis and closure (al-isti'lā' wal-iṭbāq), while zāy was used to match the ṭā' in voicing (al-jahr).

**The sixteenth benefit:** ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said they are the prophets, the truthful (al-ṣiddīqūn), the martyrs, and the righteous. It has also been said they are the believers, or the Companions, or the people of Mūsā and ʿĪsā before they altered their religion. The first view is stronger because of its generality, and because of His saying: ﴿with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisā': 69].

**The seventeenth benefit:** The i'rāb (grammatical analysis) of ghayr al-maghḍūb is that it is a substitute (badal). The qualifier (naʿt) is unlikely, because its attachment is not specific, and it follows a definite noun. It has been recited with the accusative (naṣb) as an exception (istithnā') or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

**The eighteenth benefit:** The attribution of ʿan'amta ʿalayhim (You have bestowed favor upon them) is to Allah. The anger is expressed in the passive form (lammā lam yusamma fā'iluh) out of courtesy to Allah, like His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [al-Shuʿarā': 80]. ʿalayhim in the first case is in the accusative position, and in the second it is in the nominative position.

**The nineteenth benefit:** "Those who have earned anger" are the Jews, and "those who are astray" are the Christians. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and others, and it has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). It has also been said that this is general for every one who has earned anger and every one who is astray. The first view is stronger for four reasons: it was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), the eminence of the one who said it, the mention of "lā" in His saying "nor of those who are astray" indicates that the two groups are distinct, and anger is a characteristic of the Jews in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So they returned with anger upon anger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90]. Going astray is a characteristic of the Christians, because of their corrupt differing statements about ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (peace be upon him), and because of Allah's saying about them: ﴿They have already gone astray and led many astray, and they have strayed from the right way﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 77].

**The twentieth benefit:** This sūrah comprises the meanings of the entire Great Qur'an, so it is as if it were a condensed copy of it. Reflect on it after you have mastered the sixth chapter of the first introduction, and you will know this. Divinity (al-ulūhiyyah) is present in His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. The Hereafter is present in ﴿Sovereign of the Day of Judgment﴾. All the acts of worship, including beliefs and the rulings required by the commands and prohibitions, are present in ﴿You alone we worship﴾. The entire Sharīʿah is present in ﴿the straight path﴾. The prophets and others are present in ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾, and the mention of the groups of disbelievers is in ﴿not of those who have earned anger or of those who are astray﴾.

**Conclusion:** He commanded saying "Āmīn" at the end of al-Fātiḥah, for the supplication contained in it. Your saying "Āmīn" is a verb-like noun (ism fiʿl) whose meaning is "O Allah, answer." It has also been said that it is one of Allah's names. It is permissible to lengthen the hamzah or shorten it, but it is not permissible to double the mīm. The one praying in congregation (al-ma'mūm), the one praying alone (al-fadh), and the imam should all say it during the prayer when the imam recites quietly (idhā asarra). The scholars differ about when he recites aloud (idhā jahara).
